passages.title: The Sovereign Creator's flawless, purposeful universe
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat open Sūrat al-Mulk with a single sweeping claim and then prove it: all sovereignty rests in Allah's Hand, and the evidence is written across His creation — in the mystery of death and life, and in a sky so flawless that the human eye, challenged to find a single crack in it, comes back defeated. What binds the passage together is an argument. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān maps it precisely: ayah 1 announces four divine realities — Allah's existence, His utter perfection and exaltedness, His rulership over the heavens and the earth, and His power over everything — and the verses that follow are the proofs, drawn first from the human being himself (ayah 2), then from the heavens (ayat 3–5).

## A sūrah that pleads for its reciter

Before entering the words, it is worth knowing what the Prophet ﷺ said about them. Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "Verily, there is a chapter in the Qur'an which contains thirty ayat that will intercede on behalf of its reciter until he is forgiven — *Blessed be He in Whose Hand is the dominion*." This hadith was collected by At-Tirmidhi and the four Sunan compilers, and At-Tirmidhi graded it hasan. At-Tabarani and Al-Hafiz Ad-Diya' Al-Maqdisi both recorded from Anas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is a chapter of the Qur'an that will argue on behalf of its reciter until it causes him to enter into Paradise — *Blessed be He in Whose Hand is the dominion*."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Prophetic tradition has also named this sūrah *al-Wāqiyah* (the protector) and *al-Munjiyah* (the saviour). In one such tradition, the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: "It [the Sūrah] is the protector and saviour which will rescue and redeem him who recites it from the torment of the grave" — transmitted by Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan gharib, as quoted by Qurtubi. And Ibn ʿAbbas reported the Prophet ﷺ saying, "It is my heart's desire that Sūrah Al-Mulk be in every believer's heart" (recorded by Thaʿlabi). A sūrah that will one day speak for you deserves to be understood, not merely recited.

## "Tabāraka": blessed beyond all increase

The opening word *tabāraka* comes from *barakah*, which literally means to grow or increase. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that when this word is used of Allah it signifies being highest in every respect — it carries a force similar to *Allāhu Akbar*. And the dominion — *al-mulk* — is "in His Hand." Ibn Kathir draws out what this means: Allah deals with all His creatures however He wishes; none can reverse His decree; He is not questioned about what He does, because of His force, His wisdom, and His justice. That is why the ayah seals itself with "and He is Able to do all things."

On the word *Yad* (Hand), Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the classical position of caution: the Hand is attributed to Allah in many places in the Qur'an, while He is beyond body, limbs and organs. It belongs to the *mutashābihāt* — those revealed expressions whose reality we affirm and believe in, while conceding that no one can grasp their exact nature, and that it is improper to pursue the matter further. And *al-Mulk* here, Maʿārif notes, is not one kingdom among others: it is the Kingdom of the whole universe — the heavens, the earth, this world and the Hereafter.

## Ayah 2: why death is a created thing — and why it comes first

"Who created death and life." Two things in this phrase stopped the commentators.

**Death is something Allah *created*.** Ibn Kathir notes that those who hold death to be an existing creation — not mere absence — use this very ayah as their proof, since death is here an object of the verb "created." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the question up directly: how can death be "created" if it is a negation, a not-being? The most plausible answer, it says, is that death is not pure non-existence: it is the removal of the soul from the body and its transfer from one abode to another — a real event, a positive phenomenon that overtakes a person just as life does. Ibn ʿAbbas and other leading commentators even spoke of death and life as entities — death in the form of a ram, life in the form of a mare — which Maʿārif connects to the authentic tradition that after the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of Hell have entered Hell, death will be brought in the form of a ram and slaughtered near the Sirāt (the Bridge), and it will be announced that there is no more death: every soul remains eternally in the state it has reached. Maʿārif cautions that this need not mean death is a body in *this* world; many abstract realities will be given concrete forms in the Hereafter.

**Death is mentioned *before* life.** Ibn Kathir explains one reason by linking this ayah to 2:28 — "you were dead and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die, then bring you to life" — Allah named the first stage, non-existence, "death," and the beginning of existence "life"; so death, in that sense, precedes life for every one of us. Maʿārif adds a second, more searching reason: the ayah itself declares that death and life were created *for a test* — and the test works more powerfully through death than through life. The one who thinks of death constantly is moved to righteous deeds. ʿAmmar ibn Yasir reports the Prophetic hadith, transmitted by Tabarani: "Death is sufficient as a preacher, and certitude is sufficient as a cause of being free from needs." Watching friends and relatives die is the most effective sermon there is; if that does not move a heart, nothing will. And Rabiʿ ibn Anas said that the thought of death makes a person lose appetite for this world and turn toward the Hereafter.

Maʿārif (citing Tafsir Mazhari) also opens up a wider vista: "life" in the Qur'an comes in grades. The fullest life — the capacity to recognise Allah and carry the trust of His law — belongs to the human being; its opposite "death" is disbelief, as in 6:122, where the unbeliever is called dead and the believer alive. Below that is the life of sense and movement shared with animals (2:28); below that the life of growth in plants — "how He brings the dead earth back to life" (30:50); idols are "dead, having no life" (16:21); and yet even inorganic matter has some minimal share of existence by which "there is not a single thing that does not extol His purity and praise" (17:44).

**"Which of you is *best* in deed."** Both commentaries pause on the same word. Ibn Kathir records that Muhammad bin ʿAjlan said it means best in deeds; and Ibn Kathir himself observes that Allah did not say "which of you does the *most* deeds." Maʿārif spells out the consequence: it is quality, not quantity, that counts — deeds will not be counted on the Day of Judgment but *weighed*, and the weight of one deed may outweigh a thousand. And what makes a deed "best"? Ibn ʿUmar related that the Prophet ﷺ once recited this ayah, stopped at "best in deeds," and explained: the best in deeds is the one who most abstains from what Allah has forbidden and is always ready to obey Him (cited by Qurtubi).

The ayah closes with a deliberate pairing: "and He is al-ʿAzīz, al-Ghafūr" — the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving. Ibn Kathir hears mercy inside the majesty: He is the Most Great, Most Powerful, Most Honorable — and yet, alongside all that might, Most Forgiving to whoever turns to Him in repentance after disobeying Him. The One examining us is mighty enough that the test is inescapable, and forgiving enough that failure need not be final.

## Ayat 3–4: the challenge — go looking for a flaw

Ayah 3 turns to the second proof: "Who created seven heavens *tibāqan*" — stacked one above the other. Ibn Kathir records two views on whether the heavens touch one another or are separated with space between them, and judges the latter the stronger, as indicated by the hadith of the Isrāʼ (the Prophet's ﷺ Night Journey) and other narrations.

Then comes the boldest move in the passage. Instead of simply asserting that creation is perfect, Allah *invites inspection*: "you can see no *tafāwut* in the creation of the Most Gracious" — no fault, which Ibn Kathir unpacks as no disunion, conflict, inconsistency, deficiency, flaw or defect; the whole holds together as one level, harmonious order. "So look again — do you see any *futūr*?" The early authorities glossed this word concretely: Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak and Ath-Thawri said it means cracks; As-Suddi said tears; Qatadah turned it into direct address — "do you see any defects, O son of Adam?"

Ayah 4 presses the challenge to exhaustion: "Then look again and yet again" — Qatadah said this means "(look) twice" — and your sight will come back to you *khāsiʼ* and *hasīr*. The Salaf felt the humiliation in these words. *Khāsiʼ*: Ibn ʿAbbas said humiliated; Mujahid and Qatadah said despised. *Hasīr*: Ibn ʿAbbas said exhausted; Mujahid, Qatadah and As-Suddi said the broken-down fatigue that comes from weakness. Ibn Kathir draws the picture together: look as long and as often as you like — your eye will return humbled, because it could find no flaw, and worn out from the sheer repetition of searching without ever detecting a deficiency.

A practical question: can we even *see* the sky? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from Bayān-ul-Qurʼān) addresses it: the "sky" here need not mean the blue expanse above us — the actual heaven may be far higher, the blue being the colour of the upper atmosphere, as scientists hold; and since that atmosphere is transparent, it may not block the vision of the actual sky at all. And if it were ever proven that the heaven cannot be seen with the eyes, then "casting your eye" in this ayah would refer to intellectual observation — the scrutiny of the mind rather than the retina. Either way, the challenge stands.

## Ayah 5: the lamps and their purposes

Having negated every deficiency, Allah now describes the heavens' positive beauty: "And indeed We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps (*masābīh*)" — the stars, Ibn Kathir says, some moving and some stationary — "and We have made them missiles to drive away the shayātīn."

Ibn Kathir is careful with the language here: the stars themselves are not hurled. Just as calling them "lamps" describes their function of giving light, calling them "missiles" is by association — it is the meteors beneath them, taken from the stars, that are thrown; the stars remain in place. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Qurtubi) says the same: fiery matter originating from the stars is used to shoot at the devils who try to eavesdrop on the celestial conversations, and to the common eye this burning matter looks like "falling stars." The devils are driven off before they ever reach the stars. Maʿārif also notes that the sky being "adorned" with stars does not require the stars to be studded inside the sky itself — the decoration holds even with the stars far below the heaven in space, as modern observation has found; there is no contradiction with the classical reading. Ibn Kathir connects the ayah to Sūrat As-Sāffāt (37:6–10), where the same double purpose appears: adornment, and a guard against every rebellious devil. And the ayah ends by looking past this world: this pelting is the devils' disgrace in this life, "and We have prepared for them the torment of the blazing Fire" in the Hereafter.

Qatadah's summary — recorded by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim — sets a boundary that speaks directly to the star-obsessed cultures of every age: "These stars were only created for three purposes: Allah created them as adornment for the heaven, as missiles for the devils, and as signs for navigation. Whoever seeks to interpret any other meanings for them has spoken with his own opinion, lost his portion, and burdened himself with what he has no knowledge of." The stars are signs pointing to their Maker — not oracles, and not objects of superstition.

## Living under this sky

The passage leaves the believer with a changed way of seeing. Every glance at the night sky can become what ayat 3–4 command it to be: an act of inspection that ends in worship, the eye returning humbled from a search for flaws it cannot find. And ayah 2 tells you what your own existence is *for*: not accumulating deeds but perfecting them — since deeds will be weighed, not counted — by abstaining from what Allah has forbidden and standing ready to obey Him, with death kept in view as the sufficient preacher, and the door of al-Ghafūr open whenever you fall short.

passages.title: Hell's fury and the deniers' confession
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the sūrah's first sustained scene of warning: having pointed to the perfection of the heavens as proof of Allah's power (ayat 3–5), the Qur'an now turns to what awaits those who deny the Lord behind that creation. Ayat 6–11 form a single dramatic unit — the sentence passed (ayah 6), the terrifying arrival at Hell (ayat 7–8), a dialogue between Hell's keepers and each incoming group (ayat 8–9), and the deniers' own devastating verdict on themselves (ayat 10–11). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the seam precisely: up to this point the sūrah has been presenting "evidence and proofs of Allah's consummate knowledge and power" through the created world; from ayah 6 the subject of punishment for the unbelievers (and, in the verses that follow, reward for the believers) takes over, running through seven verses before the sūrah returns to Divine knowledge and power.

## A Fire described through sound and rage

Ayah 6 states the sentence plainly: for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the torment of Jahannam, "and worst indeed is that destination" — Ibn Kathir glosses this simply as "the worst end and a terrible destiny."

Then the Qur'an does something striking: instead of describing what Hell looks like, ayah 7 describes what the condemned will *hear* as they are thrown in. They will hear its *shahīq* — Ibn Jarir explains this as "the sound of shouting" — while it is *tafūr*, simmering and surging. Ath-Thawri gives an unforgettable image for this boiling: "It will boil them just as a small number of seeds are boiled in a lot of water."

Ayah 8 goes further still: the Fire "almost bursts up with fury" (takādu tamayyazu min al-ghayẓ). Ibn Kathir explains: some parts of it nearly break apart from other parts "due to the severity of its rage and anger with them." The Fire itself is portrayed as furious at the deniers — so intense is its wrath that it can barely hold itself together.

## The keepers' question: Allah's justice on display

In the midst of this terror comes a question. Every time a group (*fawj*) is cast in, Hell's keepers ask them: "Did no warner come to you?" (ayah 8).

Ibn Kathir writes: "In these ayat Allah reminds of His justice in dealing with His creatures and that He does not punish anyone until the proof has been established against them and a Messenger has been sent to them." He anchors this in two parallel ayat. First, "And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger" (17:15). Second, the scene at Hell's gates where its keepers ask the arriving disbelievers, "Did not the Messengers come to you from yourselves, reciting to you the ayat of your Lord and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?" They will say, "Yes," but the word of torment has been justified against the disbelievers (39:71).

So the keepers' question is not a taunt for its own sake; it is the final public demonstration that no one enters this Fire unwarned. Notice too the phrase "every time a group is cast therein" — the question is repeated for each *fawj*, group after group. No one slips in without being asked, and no one can plead ignorance.

## The confession: "Yes — a warner did come"

The answer, in ayah 9, is an admission with no escape hatch: "Yes, indeed a warner did come to us, but we rejected him and said: 'Allah never sent down anything; you are only in great error.'"

The detail is piercing. They do not merely admit they ignored the warner; they quote their own words back — they had told the messengers that *Allah never sent down anything*, and, worse, had accused the warners themselves of being "in great error" (ḍalāl kabīr). The very charge they hurled at the prophets — great error — is now revealed to describe themselves. As Ibn Kathir puts it, at this point "they have no recourse but to blame themselves," and they will feel remorseful when such remorse will be of no benefit to them.

## "Had we but listened or used our intelligence"

Ayah 10 is their lament: "Had we but listened or used our intelligence, we would not have been among the dwellers of the blazing Fire!"

Ibn Kathir unpacks the two verbs. Listening (*nasmaʿ*) means benefiting from the truth Allah revealed; using intelligence (*naʿqil*) means letting one's own intellect comprehend what the Messengers brought and be guided to following them. Their confession, in his paraphrase, is: "we did not have understanding to comprehend what the Messengers came with, and we did not have the intelligence to guide us to following them." The Qur'an here names the two channels by which truth reaches a human being — revelation received through attentive hearing, and reason honestly applied — and has the people of the Fire testify that they shut down both. Either one, sincerely used, would have saved them.

Ayah 11 seals the scene: "Then they will confess their sin. So, away with the dwellers of the blazing Fire!" The confession comes — full, accurate, and self-condemning — but it comes where confession no longer avails. The response is not mercy but dismissal: *fa-suḥqan* — away with them.

Ibn Kathir closes with a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad, from Abu Al-Bakhtari At-Ta'i, who heard it from one of the Companions, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The people will not be destroyed until they themselves confess their guilt." Punishment never falls on the ambiguous or the excusable; by the time destruction comes, the guilty themselves acknowledge that the case against them is just. The scene in these ayat is that hadith enacted at cosmic scale.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with one urgent contrast: the people of the Fire confess *there* what could have saved them *here*. Their own diagnosis — "had we but listened or used our intelligence" — is a standing instruction to those still alive: listen to what Allah has revealed before the hearing is forced, and use the mind Allah gave you on the message He sent, before the intellect's only remaining work is regret. The keepers' question, "Did no warner come to you?", reaches every reader of this sūrah — for in reading it, a warner has, once again, come.

passages.title: Fearing the Unseen Lord who knows all secrets
passages.tafsir:
## The Lord who is feared though unseen — and who knows everything

These three ayat form a single, tightly-woven argument: Allah announces the reward of those who fear Him in private (ayah 12), then declares that nothing — spoken or silent — escapes His knowledge (ayah 13), and finally seals the point with an unanswerable question: how could the One who *created* not *know*? (ayah 14). What binds the passage together is the theme of the unseen working in both directions: the believer fears a Lord he cannot see, while that Lord knows what no one else can know — the secrets of the heart.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes where this sits in the flow of the sūrah: after the opening proofs of Allah's knowledge and power drawn from His creation, the sūrah turned to the punishment of the disbelievers and the reward of the believers, a subject running through seven verses — and then, in the verses before us, "the subject of Divine knowledge and power is revisited." Ayah 12 closes the section on reward; ayat 13–14 reopen the theme of Allah's all-encompassing knowledge, now aimed directly at the human heart.

## Ayah 12: fearing Allah *bil-ghayb* — "unseen"

The key phrase is *bil-ghayb*, literally "in the unseen." The translation renders it "those in awe of their Lord **without seeing Him**" — they believe in and dread a Lord hidden from their eyes. Ibn Kathir explains the ayah this way: this is the person who "fears standing before his Lord, being frightened about matters between himself and Allah **when he is not in the presence of other people**." Reading his words, one notices that the unseen cuts both ways — such a person fears the Lord he cannot see, and he fears Him precisely in those moments when no human being can see *him*. So, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "he refrains from disobedience and he performs acts of obedience when no one sees him except Allah."

For such a person Allah promises two things: *maghfirah* (forgiveness) and a great reward. Ibn Kathir explains the pairing: "his sins will be remitted and he will be rewarded abundantly" — first the slate is wiped clean, then it is filled with reward.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir says this ayah is "similar to what has been confirmed in the Two Sahihs": the hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ spoke of seven people whom Allah the Exalted will shade in the shade of His Throne on the Day when there will be no shade except its shade. Among them he ﷺ mentioned two who embody fearing Allah in the unseen:

- "A man who is tempted by a beautiful woman of high social status, but he says: 'Verily, I fear Allah.'" — resisting sin at the very moment it is private, available, and pressed upon him.
- "A man who gives charity and he conceals it so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spent." — doing good so secretly that, as it were, one half of him does not know what the other half gave.

The first hides his obedience by refusing a hidden sin; the second hides his obedience by concealing a good deed. Both live as though the only witness that matters is the One they cannot see.

## Ayah 13: secret and open speech are the same to Him

"And whether you keep your talk secret or disclose it, verily, He is the All-Knower of what is in the breasts." The ayah does not merely say Allah knows whispered words as well as loud ones — it goes a step deeper. He is the Knower of *dhāt al-ṣudūr*, "what is in the breasts," which Ibn Kathir glosses as "that which occurs in the hearts — ideas, thoughts." The verse's logic is quietly devastating: why would whispering conceal anything from a Lord who already knows the thought before it ever became a whisper? Speech, secret or public, is downstream of the heart — and He knows the heart itself.

This is what makes the fear described in ayah 12 rational rather than superstitious. Privacy, for the believer, is a category that applies only between people; it does not exist between the servant and Allah.

## Ayah 14: "Should not He Who has created know?"

The passage closes with a rhetorical question that functions as a proof. Ibn Kathir's gloss is disarmingly simple: "doesn't the Creator know?" The One who made the heart — who fashioned its capacity to think, intend, and conceal — cannot possibly be ignorant of what passes through it. Knowledge of the creation is entailed by the very act of creating it.

And then the two names that close the ayah: *"And He is the Most Kind and Courteous, All-Aware"* — *al-Laṭīf al-Khabīr*. The pairing matters. His awareness reaches everything, down to the finest and most hidden detail — and the same One who possesses that total awareness is the Most Kind and Courteous. The believer is not being watched by a hostile inspector; he is fully known by a Lord who is gentle with him. That is why the passage opened not with terror but with a promise: forgiveness and a great reward for those who let this knowledge shape their private lives.

## Living it

The passage draws a precise picture of sincerity (acting for Allah alone, not for observers): the real measure of a person's faith is what he does when the door is closed. It asks the believer for two disciplines, mirroring the two men of the hadith — to refuse the sin that no one would ever find out about, and to do the good deed that no one will ever praise. And it removes the last refuge of self-deception: even the unspoken thought is already known to *al-Laṭīf al-Khabīr*. From here the sūrah turns, in ayah 15, to Allah's kindness made visible — the earth made subservient, its paths open, His provision spread out for those who walk in them.

passages.title: Earth made tame, yet security is an illusion
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat hold up the ground beneath your feet and ask you to look at it twice. In ayah 15, the earth is a gift — tamed, smoothed, spread with provision, made safe enough to walk on and build on. In ayat 16–17 the very same earth becomes a question: *do you feel secure?* The floor that carries you could swallow you; the sky that shelters you could hurl stones. Ayah 18 then closes the argument with history: nations before them rejected, and they were destroyed. What binds the passage together is a single truth seen from two sides — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, Allah has granted the earth its balanced structure, and He retains the power to make it swallow those living on its surface.

## The earth made tame: the image inside *dhalūl*

Ayah 15 says Allah made the earth *dhalūl* for you. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up this word beautifully: *dhalūl* means "submissive", and when Arabs used it of an animal, it meant a mount that is not insolent when ridden — a beast fully broken in. The next phrase completes the picture: "so walk in its *manākib*." *Manākib* is the plural of *mankib*, "shoulder" — in an animal, the upper part of the front legs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the point: a rider normally sits on an animal's back or neck, never its shoulders. An animal that will let you ride even on its shoulders is utterly docile. The earth, then, is pictured as a great beast so perfectly tamed for us that we may clamber anywhere upon it — even its "shoulders" — without it throwing us off.

The early commentators read the word in the same practical direction. Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, As-Suddi and Qatadah all said *manākibihā* means the earth's outermost borders, its roads and its regions: travel wherever you wish, frequent its countrysides in your journeys to seek earnings and trade.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a reflection on what this taming actually consists of, and it repays slow reading. The earth is not liquid like water, or man could not live on it. It is not mud or slime. Nor is it hard like rock or iron — for then no field could be ploughed, no well or river dug, no trench cut for the foundations of great buildings. It sits at exactly the balance where crops grow, foundations hold, and a person walking its surface does not slip. Ibn Kathir describes the same favour: Allah made the earth a stable abode, set mountains in it, caused springs to gush from it, fashioned pathways, and placed in it fertile ground for fruit and vegetation. What we experience as ordinary, unremarkable ground is in fact a continuous, deliberate kindness.

## Walk, eat — but know Who provides

The ayah gives two commands and one destination: walk in its paths, eat of His provision, "and to Him is the resurrection."

Ibn Kathir draws from the pairing of "walk" and "eat of *His* provision" a principle that runs through the whole Islamic understanding of work: striving by using the means does not negate dependence upon Allah (*tawakkul* — trusting reliance on Him). Your efforts will not benefit you anything unless Allah makes matters easy for you. He then cites the hadith which Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿUmar bin Al-Khattab, that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "If you would trust in Allah as He truly should be trusted in, He would surely provide for you as He provides for the birds. They set out in the morning with empty stomachs and return in the evening with full stomachs." At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasaʼi and Ibn Majah all recorded this hadith, and At-Tirmidhi graded it "Hasan Sahih." Ibn Kathir's comment on it is the key: the bird still goes out searching, morning and evening, for its sustenance while depending upon Allah — trust in Allah is not sitting still, and working for a living is not distrust. The two belong together. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān even suggests that "walk in its paths… and eat of His provision" hints at commercial travel — trade journeys for import and export are among the doors Allah has opened for livelihood.

Then comes the hinge of the whole passage: *wa ilayhi-n-nushūr* — "and to Him is the resurrection." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states its force plainly: man is permitted to draw the benefits of eating, drinking and living from the earth, but he must not become neglectful of death and the life after death. Eventually he leaves this world; while living on the earth he must prepare for what follows it. Enjoy the tamed earth — but remember it is a road, not a home. And, Maʿārif adds, the very next verse warns that Divine punishment can overtake a person even *before* he leaves the earth.

## "Do you feel secure?" — the same earth, unleashed

Ayat 16–17 turn the gift over and show its other face. "Do you feel secure that He Who is over the heaven will not cause the earth to sink with you, and then it should quake? Or do you feel secure that He Who is over the heaven will not send against you a *ḥāṣib*?"

Notice what the questions do. The first takes the ground itself — the *dhalūl*, the docile mount of ayah 15 — and asks: what if it stops being tame? Ibn Kathir explains "then it should quake" as the earth moving back and forth, disrupted. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the connection to the previous verse explicit: though Allah has given the earth such a balanced structure that man cannot even enter it without digging, He has the power to make it swallow whole communities living on its surface. The balance we stand on, in other words, is something He granted — and He remains fully able to take it away.

The second question comes from above: the *ḥāṣib*, which Ibn Kathir explains as a wind carrying gravel that will strike you — Maʿārif renders it a violent wind loosed with stones. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah says the same elsewhere: "Do you then feel secure that He will not cause a side of the land to swallow you up, or that He will not send against you a violent sandstorm? Then, you shall find no trustee" (17:68). Danger from below, danger from above — and, as that ayah concludes, "you shall find no trustee."

The passage speaks of Allah as "He Who is over the heaven" — that is Ibn Kathir's rendering of the phrase; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "Him who is in the sky."

There is a surprising note in Ibn Kathir's reading of these threat-verses: he calls them "another indication of His gentleness and His mercy with His creatures." How is a threat mercy? Because Allah *is able* to punish — some of His creatures disbelieve in Him and worship others besides Him — "yet He is forbearing, He pardons, and He gives respite for an appointed time without hastening." Ibn Kathir cites: "And if Allah were to punish men for that which they earned, He would not leave a moving creature on the surface of the earth; but He gives them respite to an appointed term" (35:45). Every calm day on a quiet earth is not evidence that the warning is empty; it is evidence that the One warning is patient. The question "do you feel secure?" is asked precisely so that the answer can change before it is too late. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it with quiet urgency: soon the deniers will realise how true the Divine warning was, but by then it will be too late — *now*, while they are safe, sound and secure, is the time to give it thought. That is the force of the closing line of ayah 17: "Then you shall know how has been My warning" — Ibn Kathir glosses it, "how is My admonition and what will happen to those who disregard and reject it."

## Ayah 18: the argument from history

The passage does not leave the threat hypothetical. "And indeed those before them rejected — then how terrible was My reproach?" Ibn Kathir explains: the previous nations and old generations that have passed denied, and Allah's *nakīr* — His rebuke and punishment of them — "was great, severe and painful." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the purpose of the verse: the former nations who denied and rejected the truth were annihilated by the Divine scourge, and every person needs to draw a lesson from the punishment meted out to them. The warning is not abstract; history has already shown what it looks like when it lands.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that after this the surah turns back to its central theme — the description of the forms and functions of Allah's creation as proof of His Oneness, His knowledge and His power — moving next (ayah 19) from the earth beneath to the birds that fly in the atmosphere above.

## Living between the two truths

This passage trains a believer to hold two things at once, without letting either cancel the other. The earth is genuinely tame: so walk it, trade on it, plant it, build on it, eat from it — gratefully, and with the bird's kind of *tawakkul*, going out to seek provision while knowing it comes from Allah. And its tameness is a grant from Him, held under His power: so never let its calm lull you into the false security these ayat dismantle. The one destination printed on every path across its shoulders is the same: "and to Him is the resurrection." The wise traveller enjoys the mount — and prepares for the arrival.

passages.title: Signs of the Merciful and challenges to deniers
passages.tafsir:
## One sign in the sky, then a barrage of questions

This passage pivots the sūrah from a single, tender sign of Allah's mercy — the birds suspended overhead — into a rapid series of challenges hurled at those who deny Him: who will defend you? who will feed you? which of the two walkers is guided? who gave you your very senses? What binds ayat 19–24 together is a single argument: everything the denier stands on — safety, sustenance, guidance, even the eyes and ears he uses to deny — is held in Allah's hand from moment to moment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the hinge explicitly: up to ayah 19 the sūrah has been surveying the created world as evidence of Allah's existence, oneness, knowledge and power; from ayah 20 onward the deniers are warned of the consequences of ignoring that evidence.

## Ayah 19 — the birds, and why they matter

"Do they not see the birds above them, spreading out their wings and folding them in? None upholds them except the Most Gracious (al-Raḥmān)."

Ibn Kathir explains the two verbs: *ṣāffāt* is the bird with wings outspread, gliding on the air; *yaqbiḍn* is the drawing in and beating of the wings in flight. Both states — stillness and motion — happen in the same emptiness, and in both "none upholds them except the Most Gracious": Allah holds them aloft by subjecting the air to them, out of His mercy and His gentleness. Ibn Kathir links this to the similar ayah in Sūrat al-Naḥl (16:79), where the birds "held in the midst of the sky" are called clear signs for people who believe.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this sign is chosen. Birds are heavy bodies; by the law of gravity, weighty bodies released from above should fall to the earth. They have no intellect, yet Allah taught them the art of making the air carry their weight — designing the wing for exactly this work and teaching the creature how to use it. The everyday miracle overhead is thus a threefold act of divine power: enabling the air to bear them, shaping the wing, and instructing the bird.

Notice which name appears: not simply "Allah" but **al-Raḥmān** — rendered "the Most Gracious" in Ibn Kathir and "the Rahman (the All-Merciful)" in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — the very name that recurs in the challenge of the next ayah. The bird hangs in the sky by His mercy and His gentleness. And the ayah closes, "Verily, He is the All-Seer of everything": Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah's complete sight of what is beneficial and suitable for all of His creatures. The context matters too: this ayah follows directly on the warnings of ayat 16–18 (the earth made to sink, the stone-bearing wind). Ibn Kathir reads the sequence as a display of Allah's gentleness — He is able to punish those who disbelieve in Him and worship others besides Him, "yet He is forbearing, He pardons, and He gives respite for an appointed time without hastening," citing 35:45: were Allah to punish people for what they earned, He would not leave a moving creature on the surface of the earth.

## Ayat 20–21 — two questions that dismantle false reliance

Ayah 20: "Who is it besides the Most Gracious that can be an army to you, to help you? The disbelievers are in nothing but delusion (*ghurūr*)." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here addresses the idolaters who seek help and sustenance from others besides Him, rebuking them for what they believe and informing them that they will never attain what they hope for: there is no protector or helper besides Him. This is why the ayah declares the disbelievers to be "in nothing but delusion." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it starkly: if Allah decides to punish a nation, there is no power in the world that can stop Him — no fighting force, no army of soldiers, can come to the disbelievers' support and save them.

Ayah 21 moves from protection to provision: "Who is it that can provide for you if He should withhold His provision?" Ibn Kathir's comment closes every escape route: "There is no one who gives, withholds, creates, provides and helps other than Allah alone, Who has no partner" — and, he adds pointedly, *they know this*, yet still worship others besides Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds the question in the concrete: the sustenance Allah grants by sending down rain from the clouds and by growing plants and vegetation in the earth is not anyone's personal property; it is a gift and bounty from Allah, and if He wills, He can withhold it.

The ayah ends with the deniers' response to all this: "Nay, but they continue (*lajjū*) to be in pride (*ʿutuww*), and flee (*nufūr*)." Ibn Kathir: they persist in transgression, lying and misguidance; they continue in obstinacy and arrogance, fleeing from the truth — they will neither listen to it nor follow it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: they neither consider the Signs of Allah nor pay heed to other people's good advice, obstinately persisting in insolence and deviation from the Truth. The problem, in other words, is not lack of evidence but refusal.

## Ayah 22 — the two walkers

"Is he who walks prone on his face, more rightly guided, or he who walks upright on a straight path?"

Ibn Kathir calls this a parable Allah has made of the believer and the disbeliever. The disbeliever is like a man moving bent over, face toward the ground: he does not know where he is going or how; he is lost, astray and confused. The believer walks erect on a clear path — and Ibn Kathir adds a beautiful detail: "he is straight within himself while his path is straight as well." Uprightness of posture and uprightness of way mirror each other; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān confirms that "the one who walks on a straight path" is the believer who is rightly guided.

Then Ibn Kathir takes the parable further: this is their likeness in this world, and their likeness will be the same in the Hereafter. On the Day of Judgement the believer will be gathered walking upright upon the straight path, with the vast and spacious Paradise opened up for him, while the disbeliever will be gathered walking down on his face to the Hellfire. Here both commentaries cite the same hadith of Anas ibn Malik: the Companions asked, "O Messenger of Allah, how will the people be gathered on their faces?" and the Prophet ﷺ replied, "Is not He who made them to walk on their legs able to make them walk on their faces?" Ibn Kathir records it from Imam Ahmad and notes it is also recorded in the Two Sahihs; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise records it from Bukhari and Muslim.

## Ayat 23–24 — the argument turns inward

Having pointed to the sky (ayah 19) and to livelihood (ayat 20–21), the challenge now turns to the denier's own body. Ayah 23: "Say: It is He Who has created you, and endowed you with hearing and seeing, and hearts. Little thanks you give." Ibn Kathir: He initiated your creation when you were not even a thing worth mentioning, and the "hearts" (*afʼidah*) mean intellects and powers of reasoning.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on why exactly these three are named. Of the five senses the philosophers count — smell, taste, touch, hearing, sight — only hearing and sight are mentioned, because man receives a very limited range of knowledge by smelling, tasting and feeling; he depends for information largely on hearing and seeing. And hearing is placed *before* sight, because, on careful analysis, most of the information gathered in human life comes through hearing rather than seeing. The third organ is the heart, named because it is the centre of knowledge: what the ears and eyes gather depends on the heart — a view the commentary contrasts with the philosophers and scientists who locate the centre of knowledge in the brain. The verse's closing rebuke, "little thanks you give," is explained by Ibn Kathir not as a failure to say thank-you but as a failure of use: how little these gifted faculties are actually employed in obeying Allah, acting according to His commandments, and avoiding His prohibitions.

Ayah 24 completes the movement: "Say: It is He Who has created you on the earth, and to Him shall you be gathered." Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah's spreading and distributing of humanity throughout the various regions and areas of the earth with all their differing languages, colours, shapes, appearances and forms — and then the counter-movement: you will all come together after this separation and division; He will gather you just as He separated you, and bring you back again just as He first originated you. This gathering is precisely the claim the deniers doubt in the ayat that follow ("When will this promise come to pass?"), and Ibn Kathir presents this very passage — Allah's power to create — as the evidence of the final abode.

## Living under this passage

The ayat leave the reader with a simple audit. The safety you assume, the provision you eat, the direction you walk in, the ears, eyes and heart you are reading with — every one of them is upheld by al-Raḥmān, the Most Gracious, the way the bird is upheld mid-air. The passage asks that these gifted faculties be used as Ibn Kathir describes their purpose — in obeying Allah, following His commandments and avoiding what He prohibited — rather than in *ʿutuww* and *nufūr*, obstinacy and flight from the truth. And it fixes the destination: the scattering across the earth ends in a gathering before Allah, walking either upright on a straight path or in the posture of the one who refused to look up.

passages.title: The mocking question 'When?' and its answer
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move as one unit: a question is put to the Prophet ﷺ — "When will this promise come to pass?" (ayah 25) — the Prophet ﷺ is given his answer (ayah 26), and then the Qur'an carries us forward to the Day itself, when the question is answered not in words but in reality, before the very eyes of those who asked it (ayah 27). What binds the three together is that single word, "When?" — asked in this world by those who denied, and answered finally in the next.

## Why the question is asked here

The demand of ayah 25 does not come out of nowhere. Ibn Kathir reads it as the direct response to the verse just before it, where Allah says, "It is He Who has created you on the earth, and to Him shall you be gathered" (ayah 24). Having heard that the scattered peoples of the earth — with all their "differing languages, colors, shapes, appearances and forms," as Ibn Kathir puts it — will one day be brought back together before their Creator, the disbelievers respond: "When will this promise come to pass, if you are telling the truth?" Ibn Kathir explains their intent: "when will this gathering after separation that you are informing us of, occur?"

Notice what kind of question this is. It is not the question of a seeker who wants to prepare. The condition tacked onto the end — "if you are telling the truth" — shows that the askers have already decided the answer. Ibn Kathir introduces them as "the disbelievers who reject the final return, and doubt concerning its real occurrence." They treat the absence of a date as grounds for doubting the promise itself. The rest of the passage dismantles exactly that assumption.

## The two "only"s of ayah 26

The Prophet ﷺ is commanded to answer, and his answer turns on two restrictions — in Arabic, the word *innamā*, "only," used twice in one short verse.

**"The knowledge is with Allah only."** Ibn Kathir explains: "no one knows the time of the Day of Judgement exactly except Allah, but He has commanded me to inform you that it is real and it will definitely occur, so beware of it." This is the decisive point of the whole passage. The questioners wanted to make the *timing* the test of truth; the answer separates the two completely. The *fact* of the Day is certain and has been conveyed; the *time* of the Day belongs to Allah's own knowledge and was never part of the Prophet's ﷺ commission. Not knowing "when" is therefore no argument against "whether."

**"I am only a plain warner."** The second restriction defines the Prophet's ﷺ role with the same precision. In Ibn Kathir's words: "I am only obligated to convey, and verily I have performed my duty (of conveying) towards you." He is a *nadhīr mubīn* — a warner whose warning is plain, open, and unambiguous. He is not the keeper of Allah's timetable, and he is not responsible for forcing anyone to believe. Once the warning has been clearly delivered, his duty is discharged — and the burden shifts entirely onto those who heard it.

## When "when?" is finally answered

Ayah 27 then does something devastating: it answers the question by showing the questioners the answer. "But when they will see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieve will be sad and grievous." The word rendered "approaching" (*zulfatan*) pictures the thing drawing near — no longer a report to be debated, but a sight filling their eyes.

Ibn Kathir unfolds the scene. When the Day of Judgement begins and the disbelievers witness it, "they see that the matter has drawn close, because everything that is to occur will occur, even if it takes a long time." That single clause quietly refutes their whole challenge: distance in time was never safety. And the grief on their faces is not mere surprise; it is recognition. "When what they denied occurs, it will grieve them because they will know what is awaiting them there (in Hell) of the worst evil." Ibn Kathir adds that it will surround them, and Allah will bring upon them "what they were not able to reckon or fully comprehend" — and he links this to Allah's words elsewhere: "And there will appear to them from Allah that which they had not taken into account" (39:47–48). They had counted on a world without a reckoning; the reckoning arrives carrying what they never took into account.

Then comes the final word of the passage — and it is aimed straight back at the question of ayah 25: "This is what you were calling for!" Ibn Kathir says this will be said to them "in order to scold and reprimand them," and glosses it: this is what "you were seeking to hasten." The symmetry is exact and terrible. They asked "When?" as though demanding delivery of something they did not believe existed. On that Day it is placed in front of them, with the reminder that they themselves kept calling for it.

## What the passage asks of a believer

Two attitudes flow directly from this exchange, and both come from ayah 26.

First, hold together certainty and reserve in the right places. The believer is *certain* that the gathering will happen — "it is real and it will definitely occur, so beware of it" — while making no claim at all about its date, because that knowledge is with Allah alone. Anyone who reverses this, treating the unknown date as grounds for doubt, is repeating the error of the questioners of ayah 25.

Second, understand what conveying the truth does and does not involve. The Prophet ﷺ himself was "only a plain warner": his obligation was to deliver the message clearly, not to produce dates on demand or to compel acceptance. The warning in this passage has been delivered plainly. Ayah 27 shows what it will mean, on that Day, to have heard it and rejected it.

passages.title: Final retorts: trust the Merciful, source of life
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the closing words of Sūrah al-Mulk — three commands to the Prophet ﷺ, each beginning with *qul*, "Say." Together they form his final retorts to the idolaters: your hopes for our destruction will not save you (ayah 28); our trust is in the Most Gracious, and you will come to know who is truly astray (ayah 29); and if you doubt your dependence on Him, consider the water beneath your feet (ayah 30). What binds the passage into one unit is the theme of misplaced hope versus true reliance: the disbelievers pinned their hopes on the destruction of the believers, while the believers pinned theirs on the Most Gracious who alone gives — and can withhold — the very sources of life.

## Ayah 28: "Your hopes for our destruction will not rescue you"

Ibn Kathir explains that this ayah is addressed "to these idolators who are associating partners with Allah and denying His favors." They hoped that torment and exemplary punishment would strike the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. Ayah 28 dismantles that hope with a single question: *whether Allah destroys me and those with me, or shows us mercy — who will save the disbelievers from a painful torment?*

The logic is piercing. The fate of the believers — whichever way it goes — changes nothing about the fate of those who reject Allah. As Ibn Kathir puts it, the meaning is: "save yourselves, for verily, there is nothing that can rescue you from Allah except repentance, turning to Him for forgiveness and returning to His religion. Your hopes that torment and exemplary punishment will strike us, will not benefit you. Whether Allah punishes us or has mercy on us, there is no escaping from Allah's punishment and painful torment that you will suffer." The heading Ibn Kathir gives this section captures it exactly: *the death of the believer will not save the disbeliever, so let him reflect upon his own deliverance.* The only door out is repentance — and it stands open.

## Ayah 29: The believer's creed in one line

Having turned the disbelievers' attention to their own peril, the next "Say" states positively what the believers stand upon: **"He is the Most Gracious — in Him we believe, and upon Him we rely."**

Two verbs carry the whole religion here: *āmannā* (we believe) and *tawakkalnā* (we rely). Ibn Kathir glosses it: "we believe in the Lord of all that exists, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, and upon Him we rely in all of our affairs" — and he notes that this pairing of worship and reliance echoes Allah's words elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"So worship Him and rely upon Him"* (11:123). Faith in the heart and dependence in practice belong together; the ayah declares both in the face of a hostile audience.

Then comes the quiet, confident warning: *"So you will come to know who it is that is in manifest error."* The dispute between the Prophet ﷺ and his opponents will not be settled by argument alone but by outcome. Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: you will come to know, "between Us and you," to whom the final end — ultimate victory — will belong, in this life and in the Hereafter.

## Ayah 30: The final question — who brings you water?

The sūrah then closes with one last "Say," and it is deliberately concrete. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that towards the end of the sūrah, after the disbelievers are threatened with punishment, this reminder is once again repeated to them — and its final proof is the most everyday thing imaginable: **water**.

*"Tell me: if your water were to sink away, who then could bring you flowing water?"*

The Arabic turns on two opposed words. **Ghawr** (from *ghāʾir*, "sinking") means water that has vanished into the depths of the earth. Ibn Kathir explains: if it were to disappear "into the lowest depths of the earth, then it would not be reachable with iron axes nor strong arms" — no tool and no muscle could retrieve it. And he notes that *ghāʾir* here is "the opposite of springing forth." Its counterpart is **maʿīn**: water that is "springing forth, flowing, running upon the face of the earth" — water at the surface, alive and within reach. The whole verse hangs between these two words: water sunk beyond recovery, or water flowing freely at your feet — and no one is able to bring it forth except Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out how immense a favour this is. The water people casually draw from wells is not their personal property but a Divine gift. Allah sent the water down, stored it as ice on the peaks of mountains so it would not putrefy, then caused it to melt gradually and seep through the mountains' pores until a network of water spread beneath the whole earth — "without any pipeline." Whenever a person needs it, he can dig a few metres down and water is waiting. And the same commentary presses the closing question: if all of it were to vanish into the depths, "do they have any power through which they will be able to obtain pure running water?" Obviously, the answer is in the negative.

Ibn Kathir ends on gratitude: it is "merely out of His favor and His grace" that He causes water to spring forth and run to the various regions of the earth "in an amount that is suitable for the needs of servants, be it little or abundant. So Allah's is all the praise and thanks."

## Answering the verse's question

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that it is recorded in a Tradition that when a person recites this final verse, he should say: **اللہُ رَبُّ العَالَمِینَ** — *"Allah, the Lord of the worlds."* That is: it is Allah alone who can bring the water back; none of us has the power.

## Living the close of al-Mulk

The passage leaves the believer with three postures. First, do not measure truth by worldly fortunes — the death of the believer will not save the disbeliever; each soul must look to its own deliverance, and the door named in ayah 28 is repentance, seeking forgiveness, and returning to Allah's religion. Second, make ayah 29 your stance under pressure: belief and reliance upon Allah in all of one's affairs, declared together, leaving the final outcome to Allah in this life and the Hereafter. Third, let ayah 30 retrain your eyes: the water in the well and the spring is held there only by Allah's favour and grace — "so Allah's is all the praise and thanks." It is fitting that both commentaries close the sūrah here in exactly that spirit: Ibn Kathir ends with "all praise and thanks are due to Allah," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends with *al-ḥamdulillāh* — praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.
